clue.text: Pilot has relocated, getting better place

indicators.note: Anything relocated has been picked up and set down somewhere else, and these letters move the same way.

parts.note: eight letters to work from, exactly the count the grid wants

explanation.surface: A pilot who has moved house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relocated' sits in the surface as a fact about the pilot's address and is the instruction. The definition is a whole phrase, not a word: somewhere you go to get better.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospital is named here by what happens in it — people are taken there to recover — rather than by any synonym.

clue.text: Joker 50% down in hustings, pollsters admitted

indicators.note: something admitted is let inside, so the pollsters go into the middle of the shortened word
a word brought down by fifty per cent keeps only half its letters, here the front half of hustings

parts.note: MORI is a well-known British polling organisation, now part of Ipsos

explanation.surface: A comic candidate's support halves on the campaign trail, as the pollsters concede.
explanation.walkthrough: '50% down' halves HUSTINGS to HUST; MORI (the British polling firm) is 'admitted' into it. Hustings are election campaign meetings.
explanation.definitionFit: A humorist is a writer or performer of comic material, someone who jokes for a living.

clue.text: Not one large citrus fruit turned white

definitions.note: 'White' is the wine and not the colour, and the answer is one white grape among many, so the definition names the class it belongs to.

indicators.note: To turn a thing is to face it the other way about, so the pieces built up here are read from the far end back.

parts.note: not one of them and no to them come to the same thing
L is large on a clothing label
limes are citrus, and the plural supplies the five letters needed

explanation.surface: A crate of large citrus fruit in which not one has gone white.
explanation.walkthrough: Semillon is the grape behind white Bordeaux and Sauternes, so the last word of the clue is a noun. 'Turned' is the only word saying the three pieces are read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Semillon is a white wine grape, and a wine made from it is sold simply as a white.

clue.text: Antique coins Len traded worth nothing

indicators.note: Traded things change hands and end up somewhere other than where they started, which is what becomes of these letters.

parts.note: fifteen letters, the full width of the grid

explanation.surface: Len swapping old coins that turn out to be worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words carry all fifteen letters, and Len is in the clue only for his three of them. Swapping and trading are the same act, which is why the instruction reads as part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inconsequential has no consequences and no weight, so it counts for nothing and is worth nothing to anybody.

clue.text: Friend's gone across motorway

indicators.note: A plank laid across a gap spans it from side to side, so the word it applies to opens out and takes the next piece into the middle.

parts.note: a week gone and a week ago are the same week
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, London to Leeds, and its number is written in the grid as the letter I

explanation.surface: A friend who has crossed the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: Motorway means MI in a grid, the M1 with its figure written as a letter, and that convention is worth pocketing. 'Gone' looks like part of the friend's story and is a three-letter word for past.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend and has been at home in English since the Westerns, used for a companion or a pal.

clue.text: Son turning Dutchman out of yard — he's untidy

indicators.note: 'out of' means the yard letter is taken out of the footballer's name

parts.note: Johan Cruyff, the Dutch footballer famous for the Cruyff Turn

explanation.surface: A son, swinging round, throws a Dutch visitor out of the yard for being messy.
explanation.walkthrough: Johan Cruyff was a Dutch football great whose signature move was the Cruyff Turn, hence 'turning Dutchman'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scruff is a scruffy, untidily dressed person.

clue.text: Statistician's compared angry Irish band member with happy

definitions.note: The possessive says whose word is wanted: 'compared' is the everyday verb, and the answer is the statistician's version of it.

parts.note: cross is mildly angry, the word you use to a child
the Corrs are a family band from Dundalk, so one of them is a Corr
elated is happy at its highest pitch

explanation.surface: A statistician weighing a bad-tempered Irish musician against a cheerful one.
explanation.walkthrough: Three plain synonyms stack up with nothing hidden between them, and the band is the only real obstacle. The hyphen falls exactly where the first piece ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross-correlate two sets of figures is to measure how far one matches the other, which is comparing them the statistician's way.

clue.text: Maintenance on battlements?

parts.note: on the roof and up on the roof put you in the same place
the keep is a castle's central tower, the strong point the battlements run round

explanation.surface: A question about what it costs to look after a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two and the clue's question answers itself: a man on the battlements is up the keep. The question mark is the setter owning up to how playful the join is.
explanation.definitionFit: Upkeep is the money and labour a building or a vehicle needs to stay in good order, which is its maintenance.

clue.text: Fellow in a horizontal position doing a Superman impression?

definitions.note: The definition points at the answer through its most famous instance instead of defining the word, which is what the question mark admits.

parts.note: F is fellow, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
lying is what you are doing when you are horizontal

explanation.surface: A man stretched out flat on the floor, pretending to be Superman.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke and the wordplay are the same thing: the impression only works lying down. 'Fellow' looks like the man in the picture and is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Superman's whole act is flight, one arm out ahead of him, so anyone doing his impression is flying.

clue.text: Awful tower had grim cells

definitions.note: Death row is a whole line of cells taken together, so the plural definition names the collection the singular answer stands for.

indicators.note: An awful state of affairs is one where nothing is where it ought to be, and that goes for these letters as well.

parts.note: eight letters to rearrange, the length wanted

explanation.surface: A dreadful tower that had bleak cells inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface builds a medieval keep and the answer is a modern American prison block. 'Awful' opens the clue in its ordinary sense and is doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Death row is the line of cells holding prisoners who are waiting to be executed, which is about as grim as a cell gets.

clue.text: Act like a woman whose little hand is frozen with cold

parts.words: a woman whose little hand is frozen
parts.note: in Puccini's La Boheme, Rodolfo takes Mimi's hand and sings that it is frozen
C is cold, as marked on a tap

explanation.surface: Behaving like a woman whose small hand has gone numb in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your tiny hand is frozen' is the aria Rodolfo sings to Mimi in La Boheme, and it is the only way into the first four letters. The clue describes her rather than naming her.
explanation.definitionFit: To mimic somebody is to copy their voice and their manner, which is acting like them.

clue.text: Wrong choice crucial in rough game with sticks and blades

definitions.text: rough game with sticks and blades

indicators.note: A word spelt wrong has the right letters standing in the wrong places, which is the state these letters are in.

parts.note: six letters to rearrange
the key question is the crucial one

explanation.surface: A bad decision that proved crucial in a violent match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crucial in rough' reads as one phrase about a hard-fought game, and the definition begins in the middle of it. The blades are skates.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice hockey is played with sticks by men on skate blades, and its checking and fighting have made roughness part of the sport's reputation.

clue.text: Forbidding university jargon fills tedious course

indicators.note: Whatever fills a thing is inside it, so the letters named here are poured into the word alongside.

parts.note: a rut is the dull track a stuck life runs along
U is university, as in the name of any redbrick
lingo is the private vocabulary of a trade or a gang

explanation.surface: University jargon packed into a dull lecture course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tedious course' looks like the lecture series the jargon fills and is a three-letter word for a groove. 'Forbidding' has to be heard as the verb, not as the adjective meaning stern.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule something out is to forbid it, striking it off the list of what may be done.

clue.text: Maybe Schmidt drained his one?

indicators.note: a drained word is emptied of its contents, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: a typical German surname, emptied to its outside letters
Schmidt being German, his word for one is ein

explanation.surface: A German, perhaps Herr Schmidt, knocks back his beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drained' empties Schmidt to ST, and 'his one' is the German EIN; read whole, the clue also describes a German finishing his drink, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A stein is a large earthenware beer mug of German origin, the vessel a German drinker would empty.

clue.text: E.g. press secretary rung by no press after work

definitions.note: A press secretary is one kind of spokesperson, and the 'e.g.' owns up to the definition naming an example rather than a synonym.

parts.note: a ladder's rung and a wheel's spoke are the same bar, and the words stand in for each other

indicators.note: Work is the verb here: clay that has been worked comes out in a shape quite unlike the one it went in with, and so do these letters.

parts.note: seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A press secretary who got no calls from reporters once the office had shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rung' reads as the past of ring, with the phone in mind, and it is the bar of a ladder. 'After work' completes the office picture and is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A press secretary speaks to the media on a government's or a boss's behalf, which is one job among many held by a spokesperson.

clue.text: Man in photo with muscles cycles with passengers

indicators.note: A man in a photograph is inside it, so the letters named before this word go between the letters of the word after it.

parts.note: a pic is a photo, as in holiday pics
Ed is the crossword's stock short man, from Edward or Edwin
abs are the stomach muscles of the gym

explanation.surface: A photo of a man with a well-developed set of stomach muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gym selfie and the answer is a taxi. 'Cycles' is the definition's noun, the machines themselves, not a verb about pedalling.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedicab is a bicycle rickshaw, pedalled by its driver with fare-paying passengers in the seat behind.

clue.text: Brothers brought up unruly, none learning place

indicators.note: in a down clue brought up means read upwards, so backwards
unruly means out of order, so the letters of none are mixed up

explanation.surface: Siblings raised without discipline, none of them having attended a place of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sorbonne is the historic university in Paris, a seat of learning.

clue.text: American eagle all over American's ID

parts.note: US is American, the adjective as readily as the country

indicators.note: Paint all over a wall covers every part of it, so the letters this applies to close right round the piece that follows.

parts.note: the erne is the white-tailed sea eagle and the crossword's standard eagle
Am. is the dictionary's short form of American

explanation.surface: An American eagle spread right across another American's identity papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' is asked for twice and answered two different ways, US the first time and Am. the second. 'All over' is not emphasis: it wraps one piece round another.
explanation.definitionFit: A username is the name you log in under, the string a system knows you by, which is an ID in the everyday sense.

clue.text: Slight twitching of torso settled

parts.note: a slight is a put-down, a remark meant to belittle

indicators.note: A twitching muscle jumps without warning, and the letters this applies to jump out of order in the same way.

parts.note: five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A small tremor running through somebody's trunk once they had calmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' opens the clue looking like the adjective describing the twitch and is the noun, an insult. The answer is a gardener's metaphor for staying where you are.
explanation.definitionFit: To put down roots is to settle somewhere for good, the way a plant fixes itself into the ground it is in.

clue.text: Have lovely chat

parts.note: to have somebody is to con them out of their money
fab is the sixties' word for lovely, short for fabulous

explanation.surface: An invitation to have a pleasant natter.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words and each does a different job, the first two building the answer and the third defining it. 'Have' wants the swindling sense — you were had.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab is an informal talk, short for confabulation, which is a chat with the formality taken out of it.

clue.text: Sadist periodically traps brown bears

indicators.note: the alternate letters hold the colour word inside them, as a trap holds its catch
periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter of sadist is kept, starting with the first

parts.note: the word whose odd letters are taken
tan is a light brown colour

explanation.surface: A cruel person catches some brown bears in traps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodically' takes SDS from 'Sadist'; that 'traps' TAN (brown). 'bears' is not the animal but the verb: the surface hides it among the trapped creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something and to stand it both mean to tolerate or put up with it.

clue.text: Work can be sociable

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer's effect rather than matching it word for word: to opt in is to join in, which is the sociable thing to do.

parts.note: op is a work, as in a composer's opus number
a tin of beans is a can of beans

explanation.surface: The observation that a job can have a social side to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue passes as an office truism, and only the last two words define. 'Can' is the tin on a shelf, and op is the number printed beside a piece in a concert programme.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt in is to choose to take part rather than sit it out, which is the sociable of the two choices.

clue.text: BLT, Caesar salad? Mayo's capital

indicators.note: A salad is a heap of ingredients tossed together in no particular arrangement, which is what becomes of these letters.

parts.note: nine letters, three of them the sandwich's initials

explanation.surface: A lunch menu offering a bacon sandwich and a Caesar salad, heavy on the mayonnaise.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayo is a county in the west of Ireland as well as the jar on the sandwich counter, and the whole surface exists to keep you thinking about lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Castlebar is the county town of Mayo, the seat of its council and its largest town, so it is Mayo's capital.

clue.text: European tied knot in middle of abseil

indicators.note: the wedding word goes in between the two central letters
middle of asks for the central letters of the six-letter word abseil, its third and fourth

parts.note: the word whose central pair is taken
to tie the knot is to marry, so tied knot means wed

explanation.surface: A climber ties a knot partway down a rope descent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tied knot' suggests climbing rope but is the idiom for marrying: WED goes 'in' SE, the 'middle of abseil'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swede is a native of Sweden, a country of northern Europe, so a Scandinavian citizen.

clue.text: Attractive spies wearing buff and navy perhaps wanting uniform

indicators.note: the spies are inside the two outer pieces, as if those pieces were clothes they had on

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast or fan

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the uniform letter is missing from the colour

parts.note: navy is an example of a shade of blue
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the CIA is the US intelligence agency, an organisation of spies

explanation.surface: Spies dressed in buff and navy, out of uniform, cut an attractive figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buff' is the noun meaning a fan, not the colour. BLUE 'wanting' U (uniform) leaves BLE; CIA (spies) is 'wearing' FAN and BLE, so it sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanciable is British slang for sexually attractive, someone you might fancy.

clue.text: A little short on gasoline, land in the sea

indicators.note: A little of something is a small helping taken out of the middle of it, which is where these letters come from.

parts.note: shorT ON GAsoline, the letters running straight through two word breaks

explanation.surface: Running low on fuel and coming down in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue describe the same forced landing, so nothing in it points at a country. Hidden answers hide best across word breaks, and this one crosses two.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is an archipelago nation in the South Pacific, so its land does literally sit in the sea.

clue.text: Volcanic rock at the bottom beginning to topple

parts.note: basal means situated at the base of a thing

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, so only that one letter of what follows is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letter of topple

explanation.surface: A rock at the foot of a cliff that is starting to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the bottom' and 'beginning to' both read as position in the surface picture, and only one of them is about position in a word. Basal is the adjective made from base.
explanation.definitionFit: Basalt is the dark fine-grained rock that lava cools into, and it is the commonest volcanic rock on earth.

clue.text: Big Data Institute's announced acronym for what Big Brother keeps on you

definitions.text: what Big Brother keeps on you

indicators.note: an acronym announced is a set of initials pronounced out loud, so the three letters are spoken as the answer's words

parts.note: the institute's initials are B, D and I, which said as letter names run bee-dee-eye

explanation.surface: A research body's initials are read out as an acronym for state surveillance.
explanation.walkthrough: The acronym of 'Big Data Institute' is BDI; 'announced' says it aloud as bee-dee-eye. Big Brother is the all-seeing ruler in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four.
explanation.definitionFit: A beady eye is a sharp, watchful gaze, the close observation that Orwell's Big Brother keeps on every citizen.
